title: Permissions in an inventory tool
metaTitle: Show the floor what they can change
excerpt: Show the person on the floor what they can change, and why an adjustment is unavailable. Hidden controls feel like bugs. A locked bin should stay visible and say why.
alt: A wide city avenue with yellow taxis, tall buildings, and people on the sidewalk, a street where some lanes are clearly not yours to drive.
caption: The lane you are allowed to use should be obvious from where you stand. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Should the floor see adjustment tools they cannot use?
faqs.answer: If they will look for the tool, show it unavailable and say why, such as counts only and a lead adjusts. If they should never think of the tool, hide it. A missing button they were trained to tap feels broken, and a visible admin menu full of disabled accounting actions feels like the wrong app.

faqs.question: What should a locked bin look like?
faqs.answer: The bin stays on the list or on the scan result, with a reason. Cycle count in progress, or quality hold. Hiding the bin makes the floor think the stock vanished. They will then 'fix' the mystery by moving goods or writing a new count, which is the damage the lock was meant to prevent.

faqs.question: How should zone access work?
faqs.answer: Show the zone they are allowed to count, and name it the way the floor names it. If a scan lands in another zone, say they cannot change it and who can. Do not fail with a code after they have walked the length of the building. Say it on the scan, in the bin's name.

markdown:
Inventory tool permissions UX is how the person on the floor learns what they can change, and why something they expected is unavailable. Show the action they will look for. Say why it will not fire. A hidden button feels like a bug. On a floor, bugs become paper, and paper becomes the stock figure nobody meant to trust.

The office often wants the floor to see less. Less is fine when it is deliberate. Less without a sentence is a blank where a bin should be. The blank looks like missing inventory. People will "correct" it.

## What the floor is allowed to do

A counter, a picker, or a receiver should be able to answer three questions at the bin. Can I record a count here? Can I change the quantity the office believes? If not, who can?

Count is usually yes inside their zone. Adjust, write off, or edit cost is usually no. Those are different verbs. The screen should use the verb you mean. A single "Edit" that sometimes counts and sometimes writes off is how a permission model leaks into the stock ledger.

Put the allowed verb on the item as the primary button. Confirm count. If adjust is not theirs, do not offer Adjust as a twin button. If they have been trained to look for it, a disabled Adjust with "A lead adjusts this bin" is better than a hole. If they have not been trained to look for it, hide it completely so the count screen stays a count screen.

The W3C describes the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines as a way to keep interfaces perceivable, operable, and understandable. A control that is missing with no explanation is hard to operate, because the person cannot tell refusal from failure. [The WCAG overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) applies in an aisle the same way it applies at a desk. The reason has to be text. A lock icon with no words fails in glare and fails a screen reader on the same device.

## Hide, disable, or explain

Hide the office. Cost, margin, supplier payment terms, user admin, and bulk overwrite do not belong on a floor session. Showing them disabled is a catalog of temptations and an accident waiting for a shared login. If a supervisor uses the same device later, they can switch into a lead session that reveals those tools. The floor session stays narrow.

Disable and explain the actions the floor will attempt because the physical world suggests them. Scanning a bin in another zone. Opening a pallet that is on hold. Changing a quantity on a bin that is mid cycle-count by someone else. The scan still resolves to the bin. The bin still shows its name. The action they wanted is present and refused, with the reason.

Explain with no button when the refusal is the whole task. "This zone is closed today. Your counts are in Aisle 4." Include the path. A reason that strands them at the dock is incomplete. The next aisle, or the lead's name, finishes it.

The state you do not want is a failed scan that returns to a blank screen. Blank reads as "we do not have this," which reads as "the stock is gone." If the bin exists and they may not touch it, the bin exists on screen. Permission is not nonexistence.

## Rules the floor will actually meet

Zone boundaries. They can count Aisle 4 and not Aisle 9. Say the aisle names the floor uses, painted on the rack, not only the zone ids in the database. When a scan crosses the line, the sentence names both. You scanned Aisle 9. Your count is Aisle 4.

Holds. Quality hold, recall, or a freeze during a reconciliation. The items stay visible. The confirm action is replaced by the hold reason and the person who can release it. Letting a count proceed on a held bin, or hiding the bin, both corrupt the reconciliation. Visibility plus a refusal is the third path.

Receive but not put away, or pick but not adjust. If those are different jobs, the home task should be the job they were given, and the other job's verb should not be a swipe away. Gesture-only actions are easy to hit with a glove and impossible to discover on purpose. Put rare verbs behind an explicit control with a label.

Shared devices. The session should show whose count this is, in the header, in a name the supervisor recognizes. A device left logged in as a lead is a permission failure even if the buttons are perfect. Fast user switch, with a short PIN if you must, beats a shared "warehouse" login that can do everything.

Lead preview. Supervisors should be able to open a true floor session, with floor rights, without asking a picker to hand over a phone. If the preview still allows adjust, it is not a preview. You will sign off on a screen the floor never had.

## Say the rule before the walk

The expensive version of a permission error happens after they have crossed the building. Tell them at the start of the task which zone they are in. Repeat it in the header so a glance confirms they are still in the right session. If a lead reassigns them, the header changes and the current line changes with a sentence, not a silent reload.

Do not let them complete a long count and reject the whole thing at sync because a role changed mid-shift. If the role changes, finish the open line, tell them, and stop the next one. Discarding an aisle of honest counts because a permission flipped is how you lose the crew's trust for a quarter.

Write one sentence per rule and reuse it. The scan result, the disabled button, and the office log should describe the hold the same way. Three wordings become three policies in the argument after a bad count.

Keep the tone flat. "On hold. Ask Priya to release it." is enough. A lecture about process will not be read at the end of a shift. The name of the person who can act is more useful than the name of the policy document.

## Locked is not invisible

This is the rule that prevents ghost stock. If they cannot see a bin, they will create a new balance somewhere else to explain the cartons in front of them. The cartons are persuasive. Your blank screen is not.

Show the quantity they are allowed to know. Sometimes a hold means they may see that the bin exists and not see the number. Say that. "Quantity hidden during recount" is a design. An em dash with no explanation is a defect.

Search must follow the same rule. A search that hides held bins and a scan that shows them will be called random. The next article is about search. Permissions come first because search that "helpfully" omits forbidden bins recreates the ghost-stock problem from a different box.

Print and export, if they exist on the floor, obey the same visibility. A label printer that reveals a cost the screen hid is a leak. If the floor prints locations only, the template should not include price because the template was copied from the office.


Shared logins deserve a harder look than a visual pass. If the code is written on the sled, you do not have a permission model. You have a sticker. Prefer a badge or a short personal code the supervisor can revoke without collecting every device in the building. When someone leaves mid-shift, their code stops, and the device returns to a sign-in that shows who is about to count. The open count stays attributed to the person who confirmed the last line, so the morning conversation has a name on it.

Labels printed from the floor session should use the floor template. If a lead prints from the same phone after switching session, that template can include more, and the header should say which session is printing. A label with a cost on it, stuck to a carton that pickers can read, publishes the office cabinet into the aisle. That is a permission leak with adhesive on the back. Check the printed output, not only the screen, before you call the rights finished.
## Review with a floor session, not a founder login

Make a floor user. Scan a bin in zone. Scan a bin out of zone. Scan a held bin. Try to adjust. Each result should show the bin and a sentence you can read one-handed.

Then search for the held bin's name. It should appear with the same sentence, not vanish. That check is the bridge to [search inside an inventory tool](/blog/search-inside-an-inventory-tool). The person on the floor searches when the aisle labels and the task list disagree. The result still has to tell them what they may touch.

If the rights of floor and office should be visible in the product instead of in a training binder, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). A permission nobody can see will be treated as a broken scanner. Fix the sentence before you buy more hardware.
